newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST - HK newspaper headlines - Feb 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - HK newspaper headlines - Feb 18.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Tuesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

-- TIN TIN DAILY -- Sources close to Beijing said they had not heard any news about the health of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, which is widely rumoured to be deteriorating. But some senior officials in Taiwan believed the rumour was reliable.

-- WEN WEI PO -- Zhou Nan, director of the Hong Kong branch of China's Xinhua News Agency, urged the territory's people to support Chief Executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa and the provisional legislature.

-- Chinese-American scientist Wu Jian-xiong, dubbed "the Chinese Madame Currie", died at the age of 84. The physics expert was widely considered as one of the three greatest female scientists in the world.

-- MING PAO -- Rumour was rife in Hong Kong that all 17 Chinese directorate officials would be allowed to stay on in their posts after the handover, although Tung had not decided who would take the post of Attorney General.
-- Guangdong provincial leaders called for the strengthening of cooperation between judicial organisations in Guangdong and neighbouring Hong Kong.

-- ECONOMIC TIMES -- The new head of the Guangdong Planning Committee, Huang Waihong, said the province planned to attract at least US$12.5 billion in foreign investment this year, which would be guided towards the energy and transportation areas.
-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST -- Japan's Consul-General Hideaki Ueda said Hong Kong would become a key conduit for Sino-Japanese relations after the handover.
-- Beijing Datang Power Generation Co, which plans to begin a dual listing in Hong Kong and London next month, had cut back capacity expansion plans.

-- HONGKONG STANDARD -- A government survey showed the dispute with the United States over illegal textile transhipments appeared to have shattered the confidence of textile and garment manufacturers, Hong Kong's biggest exporters.
-- Hope remained high among insurers that enough support would be mustered in the Legislative Council to get funding for the Mandatory Provident Fund Office.
